To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
bubbles from active galacic nuclei can prevent the formation of cooling flows.
bubbles inflated by AGN can reduce the cooling flow by up to a factor of 10.
the presence of active galactic nuclei at the centers of cooling flow clusters can significantly reduce the mass deposition rate in the central regions.
In summary, our research is concerned with
understanding how hot gas is heated by active galactic nuclei in the centres of clusters of galaxies.
the role of active galactic nuclei in the formation and evolution of galaxies.
the interaction of active galactic nuclei with the intracluster medium, and how it can influence the properties of the intracluster medium and the formation of stars in the central galaxy.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
hot bubbles from AGNs are the most likely source of heating in cooling flows.
the hot, buoyant, X-ray-emission nebulae, which are inflated by active galactic nuclei, can provide the energy to prevent the formation of the cooling flows.
hot bubbles are a significant heat source in the central regions of cooling-flow clusters.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the bubbles are able to reduce cooling flows by 90% or more.
the hot gas in clusters can be kept hot by the active galactic nuclei, and thus the cooling flow problem is solved.
the bubbles are the dominant heat source in clusters and that cooling flows are unlikely to occur.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the cooling flow problem is not solved by simply adding a heating term to the equations, as has been the approach in previous studies.

bubbles are an efficient way to heat gas in clusters, and thus they can be used to explain the observed properties of cooling-flow clusters without invoking additional physics, such as thermal conduction.
the bubbles from AGN are a very important source of heat for the intracluster medium.
